content: To participate in the development of the guideline, each expert was required to complete and sign the standard WHO Declaration of Interests (DOI) form. This form, along with their curriculum vitae, was submitted electronically to the responsible technical officer. The technical officer then compiled the signed DOI forms and CVs, reviewed the information with members of the Steering Group (SG), and assessed whether any conflicts of interest existed before granting final approval for the experts’ invitations to participate. If a conflict of interest was declared, the SG evaluated its severity to determine whether it could compromise the individual’s ability to make objective judgments regarding the evidence or recommendations. To ensure consistency, the SG applied the criteria outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. All findings from the DOI statements were managed on a case-by-case basis in accordance with WHO DOI guidelines. If a conflict of interest was deemed insignificant and unlikely to affect the guideline development process or its credibility, the expert was only required to disclose the conflict during the Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting, with no further action taken. There were no cases of conflicts of interest that required additional management or assessment. The methodology and process for developing the guideline on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) of women living with HIV were overseen by the WHO Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics (CRE). Upon confirming their participation, all experts were instructed to notify the responsible technical officer of any changes in relevant interests during the guideline development process to allow for updates and reviews of potential conflicts of interest. At both the scoping meeting in January 2015 and the GDG meeting in April 2016, held in Geneva, Switzerland, members were required to openly declare any conflicts of interest to the group and submit updated DOI forms. A summary of the DOI statements and the management of conflicts of interest is included in Annex 2.3. The SG first mapped all existing WHO SRHR guidance relevant to women living with HIV, identifying gaps, overlaps, and inconsistencies to determine the relevance of existing recommendations for inclusion in the consolidated guideline. The SG identified eight topic areas requiring new recommendations or good practice statements: psychosocial support; aging and healthy sexuality; economic empowerment and resource access (including food security); integration of SRHR and HIV services; empowerment and self-efficacy in safer sex and reproductive decision-making; facilitating safe disclosure for women living with HIV who fear or experience violence; modes of delivery for optimal maternal and perinatal outcomes (specifically cesarean section); and safe medical and surgical abortion. The outcomes of this mapping exercise were presented at the scoping meeting in January 2015. The development of new recommendations began with formulating PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) questions and conducting systematic reviews of the evidence. The four PICO questions for the new recommendations addressed: (1) interventions to improve self-efficacy and empowerment in safer sex and reproductive decision-making for women living with HIV; (2) interventions to facilitate safe disclosure of HIV status for women living with HIV who fear or experience violence; (3) modes of delivery that result in the best maternal and perinatal outcomes for women living with HIV; and (4) differences in outcomes of medical and surgical abortion between women living with HIV and HIV-uninfected women. Additional literature reviews on related topics were also conducted. The quality of evidence for recommendations was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, which evaluates the confidence that the reported estimates of effect are close to the actual effects. GRADE profiles were prepared for each quantitative outcome within each PICO question, and the GRADE tables are presented in the web supplement. The strength of each recommendation was determined as either “strong” or “conditional.” A strong recommendation reflects high confidence that the desirable effects of adherence outweigh the undesirable effects, while a conditional recommendation indicates lower confidence or applicability to specific groups or settings. New strong recommendations are phrased as “WHO recommends…,” while conditional recommendations are phrased as “WHO suggests….” Conditional recommendations require close monitoring and rigorous evaluation, with further research needed to address uncertainties. The GDG’s decision-making process was guided by a clear protocol for WHO guideline development. During the GDG meeting in April 2016, participants engaged in group discussions to draft and revise each recommendation. Initial views on the direction and strength of each recommendation were gauged through informal hand-raising, which helped facilitate consensus through further discussion. Final adoption of each recommendation, including its direction and strength, was confirmed by unanimous consensus among GDG members. Following the GDG meeting, the SG prepared a draft of the full guideline document, incorporating revisions to reflect the GDG’s deliberations and decisions. The draft was sent electronically to GDG participants for further comment, and their feedback was integrated before the document was reviewed by the External Review Group (ERG). The SG carefully evaluated the ERG’s input for inclusion in the guideline. Any modifications made after the GDG meeting and external peer review were limited to correcting factual errors and improving clarity. The final version was sent to GDG participants for their approval. This guideline includes newly developed WHO recommendations (labeled “NEW”) and existing recommendations previously published in other WHO guidelines that applied the GRADE approach. It also includes new and existing good practice statements (GPSs), with the new ones labeled as “NEW.” The five new GPSs focus on creating and maintaining an enabling environment for optimal SRHR outcomes for women living with HIV. These are presented in Chapter 3, along with remarks on key implementation considerations highlighted by the GDG. The six new recommendations (RECs) address health interventions and either introduce new topic areas or replace previous recommendations. These are presented in Chapter 4, along with remarks on key implementation considerations. For each topic area in Chapters 3 and 4, additional information is provided, including background, barriers to SRHR, components of an enabling environment, and, for new recommendations, a summary of evidence and considerations to support understanding, implementation, and outcomes. Existing recommendations and good practice statements from other WHO guidelines were consolidated into this guideline if relevant to the SRHR of women living with HIV. These existing recommendations were not reviewed or changed during the 2016 guideline development process and remain valid. The evidence base for these recommendations is not included in the supplementary material for this guideline, as it was already presented at the time of their original publication.
